title: Μνηστήρων ἀριθμός
titleEn: The Count of the Suitors — Odyssey 16.213–307
about: Father and son weep in each other’s arms, like birds robbed of their young, until Telemachus asks how Odysseus came to Ithaca. Odysseus says that the Phaeacians brought him asleep, with gifts that now lie hidden in caves, and that Athena sent him to plan the killing of the suitors; he asks Telemachus to count them. Telemachus names the numbers, from Dulichium, Same, Zacynthus and Ithaca, with the herald, the minstrel and two carvers besides, and doubts that two men can stand against so many. Odysseus answers that Athena and Zeus will be enough, and gives his orders: Telemachus is to go home and mix with the suitors, bear any abuse of the beggar in silence, remove the arms from the hall at a nod and keep two sets back, tell the suitors the smoke has marred them, and let no one, not Laertes, Eumaeus or Penelope, know that Odysseus is at home until the servants have been tested.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο, Τηλέμαχος δὲ
ἀμφιχυθεὶς πατέρ’ ἐσθλὸν ὀδύρετο, δάκρυα λείβων,
ἀμφοτέροισι δὲ τοῖσιν ὑφ’ ἵμερος ὦρτο γόοιο·
sentences.i: So he spoke and sat down, and Telemachus threw his arms round his good father and wept, pouring out his tears, and a longing to lament welled up in both of them.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is the narrator’s way of closing Odysseus’ speech: ‘so then having spoken’. κατ’ … ἕζετο is tmesis, the preverb standing apart from the verb with ἄρ’ between them: ‘sat down’. ἀμφιχυθείς is the aorist passive participle of ἀμφιχέω ‘pour around’, here ‘having been poured round’ his father, that is, flung himself on him; πατέρ’ is its object. ὑφ’ … ὦρτο is tmesis again, ὑπὸ … ὦρτο ‘rose up from beneath’. ἀμφοτέροισι … τοῖσιν is ‘in both of them’, τοῖσιν being a pronoun. γόοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic γόου): ἵμερος γόοιο is ‘a longing for lament’.

sentences.t:
κλαῖον δὲ λιγέως, ἀδινώτερον ἤ τ’ οἰωνοί,
φῆναι ἢ αἰγυπιοὶ γαμψώνυχες, οἷσί τε τέκνα
ἀγρόται ἐξείλοντο πάρος πετεηνὰ γενέσθαι·
sentences.i: And they wept in a clear voice, more heavily than birds do, sea-eagles or hook-taloned vultures, whose young the country people carry off before they are able to fly;
sentences.n: κλαῖον is the unaugmented imperfect of κλαίω. λιγέως is ‘clearly’ in l and ‘in a clear voice’ in i, the house rendering of the word. ἀδινώτερον is the comparative adverb of ἀδινός ‘thick, close-packed’, kept as ‘heavily’ (house rendering); its exact force of a cry is uncertain. ἤ τ’ οἰωνοί is ‘than birds’, with the epic τε of a general comparison. φῆναι (singular φήνη) is a bird of prey whose species is not known (‘sea-eagle’ is the shipped stand-in, 3.372), and αἰγυπιοὶ γαμψώνυχες are ‘hook-taloned vultures’. οἷσι ‘whose’ is a plural dative relative. ἐξείλοντο is the aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω ‘take out’, with a general force, and πετεηνά is ‘winged, able to fly’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα τοί γ’ ἐλεεινὸν ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι δάκρυον εἶβον.
sentences.l: So then they, a pitiable tear from beneath their brows let fall.
sentences.i: So they let pitiable tears fall from beneath their brows.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα closes the simile: ‘so then’. τοί γε is ‘they’, τοί being a pronoun. ἐλεεινόν ‘pitiable’ agrees with δάκρυον, which is a singular used for tears in general. ὑπ’ ὀφρύσι is ‘from beneath the brows’, a dative plural in -σι. εἶβον is the imperfect of εἴβω ‘let fall’.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κ’ ὀδυρομένοισιν ἔδυ φάος ἠελίοιο,
εἰ μὴ Τηλέμαχος προσεφώνεεν ὃν πατέρ’ αἶψα·
sentences.l:
And indeed, as they lamented, would have set the light of the sun,
if Telemachus had not addressed his own father at once:
sentences.i: And the light of the sun would have gone down on them as they wept, if Telemachus had not spoken at once to his father:
sentences.n: καί νύ κε with the aorist ἔδυ makes a past unreal case, ‘would have set’, and εἰ μή gives the condition, ‘if … had not’. ὀδυρομένοισιν is a dative plural participle, ‘for them as they lamented’. ἔδυ φάος ἠελίοιο is ‘the light of the sun went down’, that is, the sun set; ἠελίοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic ἡλίου). προσεφώνεεν is the uncontracted imperfect of προσφωνέω ‘speak to’. ὃν πατέρα: ὅν is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative, and is easily mistaken for it. αἶψα is ‘at once’.

sentences.t:
ποίῃ γὰρ νῦν δεῦρο, πάτερ φίλε, νηΐ σε ναῦται
ἤγαγον εἰς Ἰθάκην;
sentences.l:
“In what sort of ship now here, father dear, did sailors
bring you to Ithaca?
sentences.i: “In what kind of ship, dear father, did sailors bring you here now, to Ithaca?
sentences.n: Telemachus asks how his father can have come, with no ship of his own. ποίῃ … νηΐ is ‘in what sort of ship’, a dative of means, ποίῃ being the Ionic feminine of ποῖος (Attic ποίᾳ) and νηΐ the epic dative of ναῦς. πάτερ φίλε is a vocative, ‘dear father’. ἤγαγον is ‘led, brought’ and ναῦται ‘sailors’ is its subject.

sentences.t: τίνες ἔμμεναι εὐχετόωντο;
sentences.l: Who did they declare themselves to be?
sentences.i: Who did they declare themselves to be?
sentences.n: εὐχετόωντο is the uncontracted imperfect of εὐχετάομαι (Attic εὐχετῶντο), ‘declared, professed’: what the sailors gave out about themselves. ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (= εἶναι), and τίνες is the interrogative ‘who’.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τί σε πεζὸν ὀΐομαι ἐνθάδ’ ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l: For in no way do I suppose that you came here on foot.”
sentences.i: For I do not at all suppose that you came here on foot.”
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γάρ τί is ‘for in no way’. ὀΐομαι is ‘I suppose’, and πεζόν ‘on foot’ agrees with σε, the subject of the infinitive ἱκέσθαι, the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’. Telemachus rules out the one way of arriving that needs no ship.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A reply formula. τόν ‘him’ is a pronoun, here Telemachus; αὖτε is ‘in turn’; προσέειπε is the epic form of προσεῖπε ‘addressed’. πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’ and δῖος ‘heavenly’ are Odysseus’ stock epithets and are translated every time.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγώ τοι, τέκνον, ἀληθείην καταλέξω.
sentences.l: “Well then, I to you, child, the truth will recount.
sentences.i: “Well then, my child, I will tell you the truth.
sentences.n: τοιγάρ is ‘well then, therefore’. ἀληθείην is the Ionic accusative (Attic ἀλήθειαν) ‘truth’, and τέκνον is a vocative ‘child’. καταλέξω ‘I will recount’ is the same verb as the imperative κατάλεξον, ‘tell in order, tell over’; Odysseus is about to give a plain account of how he came.

sentences.t:
Φαίηκές μ’ ἄγαγον ναυσίκλυτοι, οἵ τε καὶ ἄλλους
ἀνθρώπους πέμπουσιν, ὅτις σφέας εἰσαφίκηται·
sentences.l:
The Phaeacians, ship-famous, brought me, who also other
men convey, whoever to them comes;
sentences.i: The Phaeacians, famous for their ships, brought me, they who convey other men too, whoever comes to them;
sentences.n: Φαίηκες is the Ionic nominative plural ‘Phaeacians’, and μ’ is με ‘me’ elided. ναυσίκλυτοι ‘ship-famous’ is their standing epithet and is translated each time. οἵ τε καί is ‘who also’: οἵ is the relative and τε marks a general truth. ὅτις is ὅς τις ‘whoever’, σφέας is ‘them’, and εἰσαφίκηται is the aorist subjunctive of εἰσαφικνέομαι ‘arrive at’, with no κε, a general clause.

sentences.t:
καί μ’ εὕδοντ’ ἐν νηῒ θοῇ ἐπὶ πόντον ἄγοντες
κάτθεσαν εἰς Ἰθάκην, ἔπορον δέ μοι ἀγλαὰ δῶρα,
χαλκόν τε χρυσόν τε ἅλις ἐσθῆτά θ’ ὑφαντήν.
sentences.l:
and me sleeping in a swift ship over the open-sea conveying,
they set down in Ithaca, and gave me splendid gifts,
bronze and gold in abundance, and clothing woven.
sentences.i: and while I slept they carried me over the sea in a swift ship and set me down in Ithaca, and gave me splendid gifts, bronze and gold in plenty and woven clothing.
sentences.n: εὕδοντ’ is the participle ‘sleeping’, agreeing with μ’: the Phaeacians carried him asleep. ἄγοντες is literally ‘leading’, ‘conveying’. κάτθεσαν is the aorist of κατατίθημι ‘set down’ (= κατέθεσαν, with the preverb’s vowel lost before θ), and ἔπορον is the aorist ‘gave’. ἀγλαὰ δῶρα are ‘splendid gifts’, and ἐσθῆτα ὑφαντήν is ‘woven clothing’. Line 231 is word for word the line 13.136, where the same gifts are described.

sentences.t: καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐν σπήεσσι θεῶν ἰότητι κέονται·
sentences.l: And these things indeed in caves, by the gods’ will, lie;
sentences.i: And these things now lie in caves, by the will of the gods;
sentences.n: Odysseus tells his son what became of the gifts. σπήεσσι is the dative plural of σπέος ‘cave’ (σπῆος), in -εσσι, with a plural for what may be one hiding-place. θεῶν ἰότητι is ‘by the will of the gods’, ἰότης being ‘will, good will’ and ἰότητι a dative of cause. κέονται is the epic third plural of κεῖμαι ‘lie’ (Attic κεῖνται).

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖ δεῦρ’ ἱκόμην ὑποθημοσύνῃσιν Ἀθήνης,
ὄφρα κε δυσμενέεσσι φόνου πέρι βουλεύσωμεν.
sentences.l:
Now in turn here I came by the promptings of Athena,
that against the ill-disposed, concerning slaughter, we may take counsel.
sentences.i: And now, in my turn, I have come here at the prompting of Athena, so that we may take counsel together about killing those who are ill-disposed to us.
sentences.n: νῦν αὖ is ‘now in turn’: from what happened to the gifts Odysseus turns to why he has come. ἱκόμην is the aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘came’. ὑποθημοσύνῃσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν, ‘by the promptings’ (ὑποθημοσύνη ‘suggestion, counsel’), a plural for a single act. ὄφρα κε with the aorist subjunctive βουλεύσωμεν is a purpose clause, κε being ἄν. δυσμενέεσσι is the dative plural of δυσμενής ‘ill-disposed’, a dative of the persons the counsel is against; φόνου πέρι is ‘about slaughter’, with πέρι after its noun.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε μοι μνηστῆρας ἀριθμήσας κατάλεξον,
ὄφρ’ εἰδέω ὅσσοι τε καὶ οἵ τινες ἀνέρες εἰσί·
sentences.l:
But come, to me the suitors, having counted them, recount,
that I may know how many and what men they are;
sentences.i: But come now, count the suitors and set them out for me, so that I may know how many they are and what sort of men.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’. ἀριθμήσας is the aorist participle ‘having counted’ and goes with the imperative κατάλεξον ‘recount, tell in order’; μοι is ‘to me’. ὄφρα takes the subjunctive εἰδέω, uncontracted (= εἰδῶ), ‘that I may know’. ὅσσοι τε καὶ οἵ τινες is ‘how many and of what sort’, with the epic τε, and ἀνέρες is the epic nominative plural of ἀνήρ.

sentences.t:
καί κεν ἐμὸν κατὰ θυμὸν ἀμύμονα μερμηρίξας
φράσσομαι, ἤ κεν νῶϊ δυνησόμεθ’ ἀντιφέρεσθαι
μούνω ἄνευθ’ ἄλλων, ἦ καὶ διζησόμεθ’ ἄλλους.
sentences.l:
and then, having pondered in my own blameless heart,
I shall consider whether the two of us shall be able to face them
alone, apart from others, or whether we shall also seek others.”
sentences.i: Then, when I have pondered it in my own blameless heart, I shall consider whether the two of us will be able to face them alone, without others, or whether we shall look for others as well.”
sentences.n: ἐμὸν κατὰ θυμὸν ἀμύμονα is ‘in my own blameless heart’: ἐμός is the plain possessive ‘my’. ἀμύμονα ‘blameless’ is the house rendering, and the real meaning of ἀμύμων is not known. μερμηρίξας is the aorist participle of μερμηρίζω ‘ponder, be in doubt’, and φράσσομαι is the future of φράζομαι ‘consider’. ἤ κεν … ἦ καὶ … is a double question, ‘whether … or whether also’. νῶϊ and μούνω are dual, ‘we two’ and ‘alone’. ἀντιφέρεσθαι is the middle infinitive ‘bear oneself against, face’; δυνησόμεθ’ is the future of δύναμαι and διζησόμεθ’ the future of δίζημαι ‘seek’. ἄνευθ’ is ἄνευθε ‘apart from’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A reply formula. τόν ‘him’ is a pronoun; αὖ is ‘in turn’; ἀντίον ηὔδα is ‘spoke face to face’, ηὔδα being the imperfect of αὐδάω. πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is Telemachus’ stock epithet and is translated every time.

sentences.t:
ὦ πάτερ, ἦ τοι σεῖο μέγα κλέος αἰὲν ἄκουον,
χεῖράς τ’ αἰχμητὴν ἔμεναι καὶ ἐπίφρονα βουλήν·
sentences.l:
“O father, truly of you great report always I heard,
that in hands a spearman you were and in counsel thoughtful;
sentences.i: “Father, I have always heard a great report of you: that you were a spearman with your hands and thoughtful in counsel;
sentences.n: ὦ πάτερ opens the answer. σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ (Attic σοῦ), depending on κλέος, which here means what was said of him, report, rather than glory won. ἄκουον is the imperfect ‘used to hear’ and αἰέν is the epic ‘always’. χεῖράς τ’ αἰχμητὴν ἔμεναι καὶ ἐπίφρονα βουλήν is accusative and infinitive after ‘I heard’: χεῖρας and βουλήν are accusatives of respect, ‘as to hands’ and ‘as to counsel’, so ‘a spearman in his hands, thoughtful in counsel’; ἔμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί, and ἐπίφρων is ‘thoughtful’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ λίην μέγα εἶπες·
sentences.l: but too great a thing you have said.
sentences.i: but you have spoken of something far too great.
sentences.n: λίην is ‘too, exceedingly’, and μέγα εἶπες is ‘you have said a great thing’: μέγα stood in line 241 of his fame and now stands of the plan he has proposed, which is beyond their strength. εἶπες is the aorist of εἶπον.

sentences.t: ἄγη μ’ ἔχει·
sentences.l: Amazement holds me.
sentences.i: I am amazed at the thought.
sentences.n: ἄγη is ‘amazement, awe’; μ’ is με, and ἔχει ‘holds’ takes it as object, with ἄγη as the subject.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ κεν εἴη
ἄνδρε δύω πολλοῖσι καὶ ἰφθίμοισι μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
Nor could it be
for two men against many and mighty ones to fight.
sentences.i: Two men could not fight against many mighty ones.
sentences.n: οὐδέ κεν εἴη is ‘nor could it be’, a potential optative with the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’; ἄνδρε δύω is the dual accusative ‘two men’, subject of the infinitive. πολλοῖσι καὶ ἰφθίμοισι is the dative plural ‘against many and mighty ones’ (ἴφθιμος ‘mighty’), a dative after μάχεσθαι.

sentences.t:
μνηστήρων δ’ οὔτ’ ἂρ δεκὰς ἀτρεκὲς οὔτε δύ’ οἶαι,
ἀλλὰ πολὺ πλέονες·
sentences.l:
Of the suitors not one ten exactly, nor two alone,
but far more;
sentences.i: Of the suitors there is not simply one group of ten, nor only two such groups, but far more;
sentences.n: δεκάς is ‘a group of ten’, and the sense is ‘not exactly one ten, nor two tens only’. ἀτρεκές is ‘exactly’. δύ’ οἶαι is ‘two alone’, οἶαι being the feminine plural of οἶος ‘alone, only’, which agrees with an unexpressed δεκάδες ‘tens’. ἀλλὰ πολὺ πλέονες is ‘but far more’ (πλέονες = πλείονες).

sentences.t: τάχα δ’ εἴσεαι ἐνθάδ’ ἀριθμόν.
sentences.l: and soon you will know here the number.
sentences.i: and you will soon know the number.
sentences.n: τάχα is ‘soon’. εἴσεαι is the epic future of οἶδα ‘you will know’ (Attic εἴσῃ), with the uncontracted ending -εαι. ἐνθάδε ‘here’ points to what Telemachus is about to say, and ἀριθμόν ‘number’ is built on the same root as ἀριθμήσας in line 235.

sentences.t:
ἐκ μὲν Δουλιχίοιο δύω καὶ πεντήκοντα
κοῦροι κεκριμένοι, ἓξ δὲ δρηστῆρες ἕπονται·
sentences.l:
From Dulichium two and fifty
young men, picked out, and six serving-men follow them;
sentences.i: From Dulichium there are fifty-two picked young men, and six serving-men follow them;
sentences.n: Telemachus begins his count with the largest group. Δουλιχίοιο is a genitive in -οιο (Attic Δουλιχίου), ‘from Dulichium’, and δύω καὶ πεντήκοντα is ‘two and fifty’. κεκριμένοι is the perfect passive participle of κρίνω ‘pick out, select’, so ‘picked’. κοῦροι is ‘young men’, the word the house keeps for the suitors as young men. δρηστῆρες is ‘serving-men’, ἕπονται ‘follow, attend’.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ Σάμης πίσυρές τε καὶ εἴκοσι φῶτες ἔασιν,
ἐκ δὲ Ζακύνθου ἔασιν ἐείκοσι κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν,
sentences.l:
and from Same four and twenty men there are,
and from Zacynthus there are twenty young men of the Achaeans,
sentences.i: From Same there are twenty-four men, and from Zacynthus twenty young men of the Achaeans,
sentences.n: Σάμης is the genitive of Σάμη (Same), and πίσυρες is the epic ‘four’ (Attic τέτταρες), so ‘four and twenty’. φῶτες is ‘men’, and ἔασιν is the epic third plural of εἰμί (Attic εἰσί). ἐείκοσι is the epic ‘twenty’ (Attic εἴκοσι). Ζακύνθου is ‘from Zacynthus’. κοῦροι Ἀχαιῶν is ‘young men of the Achaeans’. This unit ends at the comma because the whole list would otherwise run past four lines.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ αὐτῆς Ἰθάκης δυοκαίδεκα πάντες ἄριστοι,
καί σφιν ἅμ’ ἐστὶ Μέδων κῆρυξ καὶ θεῖος ἀοιδὸς
καὶ δοιὼ θεράποντε, δαήμονε δαιτροσυνάων.
sentences.l:
and from Ithaca itself twelve, all the best,
and with them is Medon the herald, and the divine minstrel,
and two attendants, skilled in carvings of the feast.
sentences.i: and from Ithaca itself twelve, all of them the best; and with them are the herald Medon, the divine minstrel, and two attendants skilled in the carving of meat at feasts.
sentences.n: ἐκ δ’ αὐτῆς Ἰθάκης is ‘from Ithaca itself’; δυοκαίδεκα is ‘twelve’ (δύο καὶ δέκα run together), and ἄριστοι ‘best’ means the leading men. ἅμ’ ἐστί is ‘is along with’, σφιν being ‘them’. κῆρυξ is ‘herald’, and θεῖος ἀοιδός is ‘the divine minstrel’, not named here. δοιώ is the dual ‘two’, with θεράποντε ‘attendants’ and δαήμονε ‘skilled’ dual too. δαιτροσυνάων is an uncontracted genitive plural (Attic -ῶν) of δαιτροσύνη, the carving of meat at a feast (δαιτρός ‘carver’). The numbers Telemachus gives for the suitors add up to 108, with six serving-men, the herald, the minstrel and two carvers besides.

sentences.t:
τῶν εἴ κεν πάντων ἀντήσομεν ἔνδον ἐόντων,
μὴ πολύπικρα καὶ αἰνὰ βίας ἀποτίσεαι ἐλθών.
sentences.l:
Of all these, if we shall meet them, being within,
lest, in very bitter and dread ways, for acts of violence you exact payment, having come.
sentences.i: If we confront all of them together inside the house, I fear that in coming you will exact payment for their violence in a very bitter and terrible way.
sentences.n: τῶν … πάντων … ἐόντων is a genitive after ἀντήσομεν ‘we shall meet, encounter’: ‘all of them, being within’. μή with the future ἀποτίσεαι is a fear, ‘lest’; ἀποτίσεαι is the future middle of ἀποτίνω ‘exact payment’ with the uncontracted ending -εαι (= -ῃ); its object is βίας, the accusative plural ‘acts of violence’ (not a genitive, which would be βίης), and πολύπικρα καὶ αἰνά is taken as adverbial, ‘in very bitter and dread ways’. The grammar is hard, and the sense given is that he will exact payment for their violence, and in a terrible way. ἐλθών is ‘having come’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σύ γ’, εἰ δύνασαί τιν’ ἀμύντορα μερμηρίξαι,
φράζευ, ὅ κέν τις νῶϊν ἀμύνοι πρόφρονι θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
But you, if you are able some defender to ponder,
consider that someone might defend the two of us with a ready-minded heart.”
sentences.i: But you, if you can think of some defender, consider that someone might defend the two of us with a ready heart.”
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ σύ γε is ‘but you at least’. ἀμύντορα ‘defender’ is from ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, and μερμηρίξαι is the aorist infinitive of μερμηρίζω ‘ponder’, here ‘think of’. φράζευ is the present imperative of φράζομαι ‘consider’. ὅ is the neuter relative used loosely as ‘that’, so that the clause reads ‘consider that some man might defend’; the connection is loose, but the sense is plain. νῶϊν is the dual dative ‘for us two’, ἀμύνοι is optative, and πρόφρονι θυμῷ is ‘with a ready heart’, πρόφρων being the house ‘ready-minded’. The unit closes Telemachus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at line 225, and again after a paragraph break in Murray’s text. τόν ‘him’ is Telemachus, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and πολύτλας and δῖος are Odysseus’ stock epithets, translated each time.

sentences.t: τοιγὰρ ἐγὼν ἐρέω, σὺ δὲ σύνθεο καί μευ ἄκουσον·
sentences.l: “Well then, I will say, and you take it in and to me hearken;
sentences.i: “Well then, I will speak; you must take it in and listen to me;
sentences.n: τοιγάρ is ‘well then’ as at line 226. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ, and ἐρέω is the epic future ‘I will say’. σύνθεο is the aorist middle imperative of συντίθημι ‘put together, take in’, here ‘take it in, mark it’; μευ is the genitive of ἐγώ (Attic μου) after ἄκουσον ‘listen to me’.

sentences.t:
καὶ φράσαι ἤ κεν νῶϊν Ἀθήνη σὺν Διὶ πατρὶ
ἀρκέσει, ἦέ τιν’ ἄλλον ἀμύντορα μερμηρίξω.
sentences.l:
and consider whether for us two Athena with father Zeus
will suffice, or whether some other defender I should ponder.”
sentences.i: and consider whether Athena together with father Zeus will be enough for the two of us, or whether I must think of some other defender.”
sentences.n: φράσαι is the aorist middle imperative of φράζομαι ‘consider’, where φράζευ in line 257 was the present. ἤ κεν … ἦέ … is a double question, ‘whether … or whether’. ἀρκέσει is the future of ἀρκέω ‘suffice, ward off’, with the dual dative νῶϊν ‘for us two’; σὺν Διὶ πατρί is ‘with father Zeus’, Διί being the dative of Ζεύς. μερμηρίξω is an aorist subjunctive of deliberation, ‘am I to think of’. ἀμύντορα is the same ‘defender’ as at line 256.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at line 240, after another paragraph break in Murray’s text: τόν ‘him’ is Odysseus, αὖ ‘in turn’, and πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’ is Telemachus’ stock epithet, translated each time.

sentences.t:
ἐσθλώ τοι τούτω γ’ ἐπαμύντορε, τοὺς ἀγορεύεις,
ὕψι περ ἐν νεφέεσσι καθημένω·
sentences.l:
“Good, truly, are those two as helpers, whom you name,
though high in the clouds sitting;
sentences.i: “Those two whom you name are good helpers, though they sit high among the clouds;
sentences.n: ἐσθλώ, τούτω, ἐπαμύντορε and καθημένω are all dual forms: the two helpers are Athena and Zeus, named in line 260. τοὺς ἀγορεύεις is ‘whom you speak of’, with a plural relative picking up the dual nouns; τοὺς is the relative, not the article. ἐπαμύντωρ is ‘helper’, from ἐπί and the ἀμύντωρ ‘defender’ of lines 256 and 261. ὕψι περ ἐν νεφέεσσι is ‘though high in the clouds’, with concessive περ and νεφέεσσι the dative plural of νέφος ‘cloud’ in -εσσι.

sentences.t:
ὥ τε καὶ ἄλλοις
ἀνδράσι τε κρατέουσι καὶ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι.
sentences.l:
who also over other
men hold sway, and over immortal gods.”
sentences.i: the two who hold sway also over other men and over the immortal gods.”
sentences.n: ὥ is the dual relative ‘who (two)’, with τε giving a general colour. κρατέουσι is taken here as the uncontracted third plural of κρατέω ‘hold sway over’ (Attic κρατοῦσι), a plural verb after a dual subject, with the datives ἄλλοις ἀνδράσι and ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι, though κρατέω more often takes the genitive. It could instead be a dative plural participle, ‘to other men who hold sway’, with ‘helpers’ understood from ἐπαμύντορε. The line completes the thought of lines 263–264: even from the clouds they are strong helpers. The unit closes Telemachus’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: The same reply formula as at lines 225 and 258, after a third paragraph break in Murray’s text: τόν ‘him’ is Telemachus, and πολύτλας and δῖος are Odysseus’ stock epithets, translated each time.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν τοι κείνω γε πολὺν χρόνον ἀμφὶς ἔσεσθον
φυλόπιδος κρατερῆς, ὁπότε μνηστῆρσι καὶ ἡμῖν
ἐν μεγάροισιν ἐμοῖσι μένος κρίνηται Ἄρηος.
sentences.l:
“Not, mark you, will those two for long be apart
from strong battle-din, when between the suitors and us
in my halls the strength of Ares is decided.
sentences.i: “Those two will not stand aloof from the strong battle-din for long, once the strength of Ares is being decided between the suitors and us in my halls.
sentences.n: Odysseus answers the doubt about the helpers. κείνω is the dual of κεῖνος ‘those two’, and ἔσεσθον is the dual future ‘they two will be’. ἀμφίς is ‘apart, aloof’ and takes the genitive φυλόπιδος κρατερῆς ‘from strong battle-din’ (φύλοπις, the din and press of battle). ὁπότε takes the subjunctive κρίνηται ‘is decided’ with no κε. ἐμοῖσι is the possessive ‘my’, so he speaks of the halls as his own. μένος Ἄρηος ‘the strength of Ares’ is an expression for fighting; Ἄρηος is the genitive in -ηος (Attic Ἄρεως).

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν νῦν ἔρχευ ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν
οἴκαδε, καὶ μνηστῆρσιν ὑπερφιάλοισιν ὁμίλει·
sentences.l:
But you now go with dawn appearing
homeward, and with the overweening suitors mingle;
sentences.i: But you now must go home at first light, and keep company with the overweening suitors;
sentences.n: ἔρχευ is the imperative of ἔρχομαι (= ἔρχου), and ἅμ’ is ἅμα ‘with’. ἠοῖ is ‘dawn’ in the dative, and the participle φαινομένηφιν has the old ending -φιν, which does the work of a dative: ‘with the appearing dawn’, that is, at daybreak. οἴκαδε is ‘homeward’ (-δε of direction). ὑπερφιάλοισιν is ‘overweening’, the house rendering for the suitors, and ὁμίλει is the imperative of ὁμιλέω ‘keep company with, mingle with’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμὲ προτὶ ἄστυ συβώτης ὕστερον ἄξει,
πτωχῷ λευγαλέῳ ἐναλίγκιον ἠδὲ γέροντι.
sentences.l:
but me to the town the swineherd afterwards will lead,
like to a pitiful beggar and to an old man.
sentences.i: but the swineherd will bring me to the town later, looking like a pitiful beggar and an old man.
sentences.n: προτί is the epic form of πρός ‘to, towards’, and ἄστυ is the town. συβώτης is ‘swineherd’, here Eumaeus, though he is not named; ἄξει is the future of ἄγω ‘lead’. ἐναλίγκιον is ‘like’, agreeing with ἐμέ and taking the dative πτωχῷ λευγαλέῳ ἠδὲ γέροντι ‘a pitiful beggar and an old man’. λευγαλέος is ‘pitiful’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ μ’ ἀτιμήσουσι δόμον κάτα, σὸν δὲ φίλον κῆρ
τετλάτω ἐν στήθεσσι κακῶς πάσχοντος ἐμεῖο,
ἤν περ καὶ διὰ δῶμα ποδῶν ἕλκωσι θύραζε
ἢ βέλεσι βάλλωσι· σὺ δ’ εἰσορόων ἀνέχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
And if they dishonour me in the house, then your dear heart
let it endure in your breast, while I am suffering ill,
even if through the house by the feet they drag me to the door
or with missiles pelt me; and you, looking on, endure.
sentences.i: And if they dishonour me in the house, let your dear heart bear it in your breast while I am ill treated, even if they drag me by the feet through the house to the door or pelt me with missiles; and you must look on and endure it.
sentences.n: εἰ with the future ἀτιμήσουσι is ‘if they dishonour me’. δόμον κάτα is κατά placed after its noun, ‘down through the house’. τετλάτω is the perfect imperative, third person, of τλάω ‘endure, bring oneself to bear’: ‘let it endure’. ἐμεῖο is the genitive of ἐγώ (Attic ἐμοῦ), in a genitive absolute with πάσχοντος ‘while I suffer’. ἤν περ is ἐάν περ ‘even if’, with the subjunctives ἕλκωσι and βάλλωσι; ποδῶν ἕλκωσι is ‘drag by the feet’ and θύραζε ‘to the door, out of doors’. ἀνέχεσθαι is an infinitive standing for an imperative. Line 277 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of βέλεσι is short by nature and has to count long at the start of the second foot.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι παύεσθαι ἀνωγέμεν ἀφροσυνάων,
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι παραυδῶν·
sentences.l:
But indeed bid them to cease from their follies,
with gentle words speaking soothingly;
sentences.i: But do bid them stop their folly, talking soothingly to them with gentle words;
sentences.n: ἀνωγέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἄνωγα ‘I bid’, and with παύεσθαι ‘to cease’ it stands for an imperative: ‘bid them stop’. The genitive ἀφροσυνάων (uncontracted, Attic -ῶν) goes with παύεσθαι ‘cease from’. παραυδῶν is the participle of παραυδάω ‘speak soothingly to’, with μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι ‘gentle words’, a dative plural. ἀλλ’ ἦ τοι is ‘but indeed’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δέ τοι οὔ τι
πείσονται·
sentences.l:
but they to you in no way
will be persuaded;
sentences.i: but they will not listen to you at all;
sentences.n: οἱ is the pronoun ‘they’. τοι is most likely the dative of σύ ‘to you’, though it could also be the particle ‘mark you’; either gives nearly the same sense. οὔ τι is ‘in no way’, and πείσονται is the future middle of πείθω, ‘will be persuaded, will obey’.

sentences.t: δὴ γάρ σφι παρίσταται αἴσιμον ἦμαρ.
sentences.l: for now to them stands by the fated day.
sentences.i: for the day fated for them is already at hand.
sentences.n: δὴ γάρ is ‘for already’. σφι is the epic dative plural ‘to them’ (Attic σφίσι). παρίσταται ‘stands beside’ means ‘is at hand’. ἦμαρ is ‘day’, and αἴσιμον ‘fated, due’ (from αἶσα ‘portion, lot’), so this is the day of their death.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: ἄλλο is ‘something else’, the object of ἐρέω ‘I will say’, and τοι is ‘to you’. ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν is ‘lay it in your own mind’: βάλλεο is the imperative middle (Attic βάλλου), and σῇσιν is the dative plural of the possessive σός ‘your own’, in -ῃσιν. It marks what follows as something to be remembered.

sentences.t: ὁππότε κεν πολύβουλος ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θῇσιν Ἀθήνη,
sentences.l: whenever of-many-plans in the mind shall put it Athena,
sentences.i: whenever Athena of many plans puts it into my mind,
sentences.n: ὁππότε κεν with the subjunctive θῇσιν is ‘whenever’, and θῇσιν is the aorist subjunctive of τίθημι with the ending -σιν (= θῇ). ἐνὶ φρεσί is ‘in the mind’, and the object and the owner of the mind are left unsaid: the sense is that Athena will put the moment in Odysseus’ own mind, which fits νεύσω ἐγώ in the next line. πολύβουλος, from πολύς and βουλή ‘plan, counsel’, is a standing epithet of Athena, translated here as ‘of many plans’ and kept apart from the -φρων epithets. This unit ends at the comma because the whole sentence runs six lines.

sentences.t:
νεύσω μέν τοι ἐγὼ κεφαλῇ, σὺ δ’ ἔπειτα νοήσας
ὅσσα τοι ἐν μεγάροισιν Ἀρήϊα τεύχεα κεῖται
ἐς μυχὸν ὑψηλοῦ θαλάμου καταθεῖναι ἀείρας
πάντα μάλ’·
sentences.l:
I will nod to you, I, with my head, and you then, having noticed it,
all the warlike armour that for you in the halls lies
to the recess of the high chamber lay away, having lifted it,
every bit;
sentences.i: I will nod my head to you, and when you have seen the sign, take up all the warlike armour that lies in your halls and put it away in the inner recess of the high chamber, every piece;
sentences.n: νεύσω … κεφαλῇ is ‘I will nod with my head’, the agreed signal; νεύσω is the future of νεύω. The infinitive καταθεῖναι (aorist of κατατίθημι ‘put away’) stands for an imperative, as ἀνωγέμεν did, and so does παρφάσθαι two lines later. νοήσας is ‘having noticed’. ὅσσα … Ἀρήϊα τεύχεα is ‘all the warlike armour’ (Ἀρήϊος from Ἄρης ‘of Ares, warlike’; τεύχεα ‘armour’), with τοι ‘for you’ as a dative of the person concerned. ἐν μεγάροισιν is ‘in the halls’, a plural for one hall. μυχόν is the innermost recess, ὑψηλοῦ θαλάμου ‘of the high chamber’, and ἀείρας is ‘having lifted’. πάντα μάλ’ is ‘every one, quite all’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ μνηστῆρας μαλακοῖς ἐπέεσσι
παρφάσθαι, ὅτε κέν σε μεταλλῶσιν ποθέοντες·
sentences.l:
and the suitors with soft words
to put off, when they question you, missing them:
sentences.i: and put off the suitors with soft words whenever, missing the armour, they question you:
sentences.n: παρφάσθαι is the middle infinitive of παράφημι ‘talk round, put off’ (the preverb shortened to παρ-), standing for an imperative. μαλακοῖς ἐπέεσσι is ‘soft words’. ὅτε κέν with the subjunctive μεταλλῶσιν is ‘whenever they inquire’ (μεταλλάω ‘ask’). ποθέοντες is ‘missing, longing for’, and has no expressed object: the armour, as the answer in the next three lines shows. The colon introduces the excuse Odysseus gives Telemachus to use.

sentences.t:
ἐκ καπνοῦ κατέθηκ’, ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι τοῖσιν ἐῴκει
οἷά ποτε Τροίηνδε κιὼν κατέλειπεν Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἀλλὰ κατῄκισται, ὅσσον πυρὸς ἵκετ’ ἀϋτμή.
sentences.l:
‘Out of the smoke I have put them away, since no longer like those
were they that once, to Troy going, Odysseus left,
but they have been marred, as far as the blast of fire reached.
sentences.i: ‘I have put them away out of the smoke, since they are no longer like those that Odysseus left behind when he went to Troy, but have been marred as far as the breath of the fire has reached.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here, and these lines are the excuse Odysseus tells Telemachus to give: Telemachus is the speaker inside the quotation, which is why Odysseus is spoken of in the third person. The quotation runs to the end of line 294. κατέθηκ’ is κατέθηκα elided, the aorist of κατατίθημι ‘put away’. ἐῴκει is the pluperfect of ἔοικα ‘be like’, with the dative τοῖσιν ‘to those’. οἷα ποτε is ‘such as once’, Τροίηνδε is Τροίην with -δε ‘to Troy’, and κιών is the participle of κίω ‘go’. κατῄκισται is the perfect passive of καταικίζω ‘disfigure, mar’; ὅσσον is ‘as far as’ and ἀϋτμή ‘breath, blast’.

sentences.t:
πρὸς δ’ ἔτι καὶ τόδε μεῖζον ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε Κρονίων,
μή πως οἰνωθέντες, ἔριν στήσαντες ἐν ὑμῖν,
ἀλλήλους τρώσητε καταισχύνητέ τε δαῖτα
καὶ μνηστύν·
sentences.l:
And besides this, the greater thing too in my mind put the son of Cronus,
lest somehow, having been made drunk, having set up strife among you,
each other you wound and shame the feast
and the wooing;
sentences.i: And besides, the son of Cronus has put this greater thought into my mind, for fear that, grown drunk and having stirred up strife among you, you may wound one another and disgrace the feast and the wooing;
sentences.n: πρὸς δ’ ἔτι καί is ‘and furthermore’, and τόδε μεῖζον ‘this greater thing’ prepares the μή clause. ἐνὶ φρεσί is ‘in the mind’, that of the speaker, Telemachus. Κρονίων is ‘the son of Cronus’. μή πως with the subjunctives τρώσητε (aorist) and καταισχύνητε (present or aorist; the forms coincide) is a fear, ‘lest somehow you wound and disgrace’. οἰνωθέντες is the aorist passive participle of οἰνόω ‘make drunk’, and ἔριν στήσαντες is ‘having set up strife’, the aorist participle of ἵστημι in its transitive sense. ἐν ὑμῖν is ‘among you’ and ἀλλήλους ‘one another’; δαῖτα καὶ μνηστύν is ‘the feast and the wooing’.

sentences.t: αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐφέλκεται ἄνδρα σίδηρος.
sentences.l: for of itself draws to it a man iron.’
sentences.i: for iron of itself draws a man toward it.’
sentences.n: A saying that closes the excuse. ἐφέλκεται is the present middle of ἐφέλκω ‘draw on, drag towards oneself’, and αὐτός is ‘of itself’. σίδηρος ‘iron’ stands for weapons: the thought is that the sight of arms leads men to use them. The quotation ends here.

sentences.t:
νῶϊν δ’ οἴοισιν δύο φάσγανα καὶ δύο δοῦρε
καλλιπέειν καὶ δοιὰ βοάγρια χερσὶν ἑλέσθαι,
ὡς ἂν ἐπιθύσαντες ἑλοίμεθα·
sentences.i: But to leave for the two of us alone two swords and two spears, and two ox-hide shields to take in our hands, so that we can rush in and seize them;
sentences.n: Odysseus returns to his own instructions. νῶϊν δ’ οἴοισιν is ‘for us two alone’, the dual dative with a plural-form adjective. The infinitive καλλιπέειν (= καταλιπεῖν, aorist infinitive of καταλείπω) is another command. φάσγανα is ‘swords’ and δοῦρε the dual of δόρυ ‘spear’. βοάγρια is a rare word whose meaning is not certainly known; the traditional guess is ‘shields of ox-hide’. ὡς ἄν with the optative ἑλοίμεθα is ‘so that we might seize’, and ἐπιθύσαντες is the aorist participle of ἐπιθύω ‘rush in’, with no object given.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δέ κ’ ἔπειτα
Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη θέλξει καὶ μητίετα Ζεύς.
sentences.l:
and them then
Pallas Athena will enchant and counsellor Zeus.
sentences.i: and then Pallas Athena and Zeus the counsellor will enchant them.
sentences.n: τοὺς is the pronoun ‘them’, the suitors, object of θέλξει, the future of θέλγω ‘enchant’, which can mean to cast a spell over the mind. κ’ is κε with the future. Παλλάς is a title of Athena whose meaning is disputed; Ἀθηναίη is the epic form of Ἀθηναία. μητίετα ‘counsellor’ is an epic nominative in -α, from μῆτις ‘counsel, cunning’, and is translated every time, as Zeus’ epithet.

sentences.t: ἄλλο δέ τοι ἐρέω, σὺ δ’ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν·
sentences.l: And another thing to you I will say, and you in your own mind lay it:
sentences.i: And I will tell you something else; lay it up in your own mind:
sentences.n: The same line as 281, which began Odysseus’ first instruction: ἄλλο ‘something else’ is the object of ἐρέω, and ἐνὶ φρεσὶ βάλλεο σῇσιν is ‘lay it in your own mind’. Here it introduces the second matter, secrecy.

sentences.t: εἰ ἐτεόν γ’ ἐμός ἐσσι καὶ αἵματος ἡμετέροιο,
sentences.l: if truly mine you are and of our blood,
sentences.i: If you are truly mine and of our blood,
sentences.n: ἐτεόν is ‘truly’, an adverbial neuter, and ἐσσι is the epic second singular of εἰμί (Attic εἶ). ἐμός is ‘mine’, and ἡμετέροιο ‘our’ is a genitive in -οιο, a plural possessive for the family; αἵματος is ‘of blood’. The condition is completed in the next lines. This unit ends at the comma because the sentence would otherwise run past four lines.

sentences.t:
μή τις ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἀκουσάτω ἔνδον ἐόντος,
μήτ’ οὖν Λαέρτης ἴστω τό γε μήτε συβώτης
μήτε τις οἰκήων μήτ’ αὐτὴ Πηνελόπεια,
ἀλλ’ οἶοι σύ τ’ ἐγώ τε γυναικῶν γνώομεν ἰθύν·
sentences.i: let no one hear that Odysseus is within: not Laertes, not the swineherd, not any of the household, not even Penelope herself. Let you and me alone learn how the women are inclined;
sentences.n: μή τις … ἀκουσάτω is a prohibition with the aorist imperative of ἀκούω, ‘let no one hear’, with the genitives Ὀδυσῆος … ἐόντος ‘of Odysseus being within’; Ὀδυσῆος is the epic genitive in -ηος. The μήτε clauses name who must not know. ἴστω is the imperative of οἶδα ‘let him know’. οἰκήων is the genitive plural of οἰκεύς, in the Ionic form οἰκῆες ‘members of the household’. γνώομεν is an aorist subjunctive, uncontracted (= γνῶμεν), ‘let us learn’. ἰθύς is literally ‘straight course, aim’; ‘inclination’ is the sense taken from the context. The sentence runs five lines, and is cut at the comma after ἡμετέροιο.

sentences.t:
καί κέ τεο δμώων ἀνδρῶν ἔτι πειρηθεῖμεν,
ἠμὲν ὅπου τις νῶϊ τίει καὶ δείδιε θυμῷ,
ἠδ’ ὅτις οὐκ ἀλέγει, σὲ δ’ ἀτιμᾷ τοῖον ἐόντα.
sentences.l:
and we might also try some of the servants, men,
both where someone honours us two and fears in his heart,
and who cares not, and dishonours you, being such as you are.”
sentences.i: We might also test some of the men among the servants, both to learn who honours the two of us and fears us in his heart, and who has no regard and dishonours you, a man such as you are.”
sentences.n: καί κε … πειρηθεῖμεν is a potential optative, ‘we might also test’ (πειράομαι ‘try, test’). τεο is the epic genitive of τις ‘some’, partitive with δμώων ἀνδρῶν ‘of the servants, men’. ἠμὲν … ἠδέ is ‘both … and’, and ὅπου ‘where’ here means ‘in whose case’. τίει is from τίω ‘honour’, and δείδιε is the perfect of δείδω used as a present, ‘fears’. ἀλέγει is ‘cares, pays heed’, and ἀτιμᾷ is contracted from ἀτιμάει ‘dishonours’. σὲ … τοῖον ἐόντα is ‘you, being such as you are’. The unit closes Odysseus’ speech.
